patient_information: A 44-year-old male rice farmer from Laos, diagnosed with type 2 diabetes 4 years previously but non-compliant with oral antidiabetic drugs or follow-up.
chief_complaint: One-month history of fever, headache, generalized myalgia and arthralgia, and a painful swelling over the left scapula.
history_of_present_illness: The swelling gradually increased in size without preceding trauma; a week prior to admission, the lesion was incised and drained at a local health centre, and the patient had been taking cloxacillin 1g four times daily, but deteriorated with high fever, chills, and severe malaise in the 2 days prior to admission.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is a male rice farmer in Southern Laos presenting during the rainy season.
vitals: Fever of 40°C (104°F), heart rate of 136bpm, blood pressure of 140/80 mmHg, and respiratory rate of 30 breath cycles per minute.
physical_exam: Patient appears septic, pale and jaundiced; left scapular region shows an erythematous swelling of 2.5 × 4 cm with pus discharging from a central wound; no regional lymphadenopathy; chest auscultation reveals bilateral crepitations and reduced breath sounds at both lung bases; heart sounds normal; abdomen soft without palpable organomegaly.
labs_and_diagnostics: WBC 16.2 ×10^9/L, Polymorphs 92.1%, Platelets 112 ×10^9/L, Glucose 20.6 mmol/L, Serum creatinine 56 µmol/L, Urea 6.8 mmol/L, AST 131 U/L, ALT 83 U/L, Serum total bilirubin 111.2 µmol/L, Serum direct bilirubin 56.4 µmol/L; Chest radiograph revealed bilateral pleural effusions; Pus culture and blood culture both yielded B. pseudomallei.
differential_diagnosis: Bacterial abscess with sepsis (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Vibrio vulnificus or anaerobes), Melioidosis (Burkholderia pseudomallei), Tuberculosis, and Disseminated fungal infection.
management_and_clinical_course: Empirically treated with ceftriaxone and gentamicin, then switched to ceftazidime after 48 hours when melioidosis was suspected; the patient improved after 7 days of treatment and was afebrile by day 14, then switched to oral co-trimoxazole to complete 20 weeks; glycaemic control was established; discharged after 21 days and continued oral 'eradication' treatment for 5 months, remaining well.

images.caption: Wound on the patient's left shoulder, after incision and drain-age of the abscess. (Side finding: hypopigmented macular skin lesions of Pityriasis versicolor (Malassezia spp.), commonly seen in humid tropical climates.)
